paragraphs.heading: What a fatty acid is
paragraphs.text: A fatty acid is a carboxylic acid attached to a chain of carbon atoms, and that chain can be saturated or unsaturated. Most fatty acids in nature have a straight, unbranched chain with an even number of carbons, anywhere from 4 to 28. One end of the chain carries a carboxyl group, –COOH, and the other end a methyl group, –CH3. The idea of a fatty acid was introduced in 1813 by Michel Eugène Chevreul.

paragraphs.heading: Fuel and building material
paragraphs.text: In some organisms fatty acids are not found loose. Instead they are tied up in esters, which come in three main classes: triglycerides, phospholipids and cholesteryl esters. In whatever form, they are an important fuel in the diet of animals and an important building material for cells. In some species, such as microalgae, they make up as much as 70% of the lipids by weight.

paragraphs.heading: Short to very long
paragraphs.text: Fatty acids are sorted in several ways: by length, by whether they are saturated, by odd or even carbon count, and by whether the chain is straight or branched. Short-chain fatty acids, such as butyric acid, have tails of five carbons or fewer. Medium-chain ones have 6 to 12, long-chain ones 13 to 21, and very long chain ones 22 or more. Most are even-chained, like stearic and oleic acid, while odd-chained ones occur far less often.

paragraphs.heading: Saturated and unsaturated
paragraphs.text: A saturated fatty acid has no C=C double bonds, and its formula is CH₃(CH₂)ₙCOOH. Stearic acid is an important example: neutralized with sodium hydroxide, it is the most common form of soap. An unsaturated fatty acid has one or more C=C double bonds. Each of these bonds can take one of two shapes, called cis and trans.

paragraphs.heading: Kinks and bends
paragraphs.text: In the cis shape, the two hydrogen atoms next to the double bond sit on the same side of the chain. The double bond is rigid and locks its shape in place, so a cis bond bends the chain, and the more cis bonds there are, the less flexible it becomes. Oleic acid, with one double bond, has a kink; linoleic acid, with two, bends more; and α-linolenic acid, with three, tends toward a hook. In a trans bond the two hydrogens are on opposite sides, so the chain stays nearly straight, much like a saturated one.

paragraphs.heading: Why the shape matters
paragraphs.text: Where fatty acids are crowded together, as in the lipid bilayer of a membrane or the triglycerides of a fat droplet, cis bonds stop them packing closely. That can change the melting temperature of the membrane or fat. Cis unsaturated fatty acids make cell membranes more fluid, while trans ones do not. In most natural unsaturated fatty acids every double bond is cis. Most trans fats come from human processing such as hydrogenation, though some occur naturally in the milk and meat of cattle and sheep.

paragraphs.heading: Counting the carbons
paragraphs.text: There are several ways to number the carbons in the chain. The scheme IUPAC recommends counts from 1 at the –COOH end. Another uses Greek letters, starting at the carbon just after the carboxyl group, so alpha is C-2 and beta is C-3, and the last carbon is always called omega. A third way counts back from that end, giving labels like ω−1 and ω−2, which can also be written n−1 and n−2.
